newsitem.title: USA: CME live cattle close weak after setting new highs.
newsitem.headline: CME live cattle close weak after setting new highs.

text.p: CME live cattle futures closed lower on profit taking and concern over cattle placements onto feedlots due to lower feed costs, traders said.
The declines in live cattle came after values set new contract highs early in October and December.
But lower corn futures supported feeders, traders said.
October live cattle set a new high of 73.525 cents and December 68.950 before slipping to close 0.625 to 0.050 lower, paced by December. Oct ended at 72.950 cents, off 0.325.
Continued strong cash markets boosted prices for the fifth consecutive contract high early, but profit taking developed.

Some traders considered futures at or near a top after recent advances. Cash cattle prices may go up another week or two, but the longer-term trend is for prices to ease as feedlot supplies start to recover from low levels the past few months. Friday's monthly USDA cattle on feed is expected to show large placements during August, they said.

Early trade projections on Friday's report for on-feed cattle supplies as of Sept 1 in the seven key states ranged from from 88.2 to 92 percent of a year ago, with the number of cattle placed in feedlots seen at 106.6 to 115.8 percent for placements and marketings at 92 to 98 percent of a year ago.
The increased pace of placements is seen persisting as feed costs ease to more normal levels.
"Lower corn prices may step up placements," said Julia Bussie, analyst for AG Edwards.
Merrill Lynch and Dean Witter notably sold October while R.J. O'Brien, RBH and Refco sold December down into sell stops, pit sources said.
Feeder cattle set new highs of 65.550 cents in October and 65.875 in November before closing 0.025 to 0.550 cent higher with October up most at 65.450 cents. Distant August also set a new high.
Lower corn futures underpinned feeder cattle futures, traders said. Recent strong demand for replacement feeders at feedlots will likely continue due to declining feed costs, they said.

Cargill Investor Services notably bought October, traders said, while Smith Barney, Prudential Securities, Refco and Cargill Investor Services were also light buyers. R.J. O'Brien was the best seller with LIT division of First Options also selling, pit sources said.
